lessons.title: Receiving a load of nuts in husk
lessons.html:
Why intake matters

Nuts in husk (NIH) arrive at the de-husking shed from the orchard, often in bins on a trailer or in bags on a bakkie. Intake is the first step in the shed. If intake is done badly, the farm cannot tell whose nuts are whose, how much was delivered or why a batch was rejected later at the processor. Good intake protects the grower, the farm and the buyer.

Before the load arrives

  • Check that the scale has been checked or zeroed as per shed procedure.
  • Have intake forms or the tablet ready, with delivery numbers in order.
  • Make sure there is clean, dry space or empty bins ready to receive nuts.
  • Know the farm's acceptance rules, for example what to do with very wet, mouldy or dirty loads.

When the load arrives

  1. Record the vehicle, driver, the block or grower the nuts come from and the date and time.
  2. Weigh the load. Record the gross weight, then the tare (empty bins or vehicle) and work out the net weight.
  3. Look at the load. Note leaves, sticks, stones, soil, fallen rotten nuts and any smell of mould or fermentation.
  4. Take a sample using the method the shed uses, for example from several places in the load, not just the top.
  5. Give the load a lot or batch number and label the bins clearly.

Safety at intake

  • Stand clear of vehicles when they reverse. Use a guide signal the driver can see.
  • Only trained operators may drive forklifts or tip bins.
  • Wear safety shoes and a reflective vest in the yard.
  • Lift bags correctly, bending the knees, and share heavy loads.

lessons.title: Sampling, quality checks and storage
lessons.html:
Checking quality

The sample tells the farm how good the load is. Processors pay for sound kernel, so the shed needs to know early if there is a problem.

Common checks on a sample

  • Foreign matter – weigh out leaves, sticks and stones.
  • Moisture – nuts in husk are wet. Use the moisture meter or oven method as the shed's procedure says. Wet nuts must be de-husked and dried quickly.
  • Damaged nuts – crack a set number and look for insect damage, stink bug marks, mould, germination and immature kernel.
  • Husk condition – rotten or black husks may mean nuts lay too long on the ground.

Record all results against the lot number. Compare them with the acceptance limits the farm or buyer has set. If a load fails, set it aside, label it clearly and tell your supervisor. Do not mix it with good nuts.

Storing nuts in husk

  • De-husk as soon as possible. Nuts left in wet husk heat up, go mouldy and lose quality.
  • If nuts must wait, keep them in shallow layers or ventilated bins in the shade, out of rain.
  • Keep each lot separate and labelled. Work first in, first out.
  • Keep rats and birds out. Report droppings or gnawed bags.

Traceability

Many buyers ask the farm to trace every batch back to the block it came from. Your intake record is the first link in that chain. Write clearly, never leave blanks and sign the form. If you make a mistake, cross it out neatly and write the correct value next to it; do not tear out pages.

Key points

  • Record source, date, weights and a lot number for every load.
  • Sample from several places in the load, not just the top.
  • Check foreign matter, moisture and damaged nuts against the limits.
  • Set aside and label loads that fail; never mix them with good nuts.
  • De-husk wet nuts quickly and keep lots separate.

quiz.question: How do you work out the net weight of a load?

options.text: Add the tare to the gross weight
Subtract the tare (empty bins or vehicle) from the gross weight
Weigh only a sample
Use the weight written by the driver

quiz.question: Where should you take a sample from a load of nuts in husk?

options.text: Only from the top of the load
Only from the cleanest bin
From several places in the load
From the floor of the shed

quiz.question: What should you do with a load that fails the acceptance limits?

options.text: Set it aside, label it and tell your supervisor
Mix it with a good load to hide the problem
Send it straight to the buyer
Throw it in the veld

quiz.question: Why should nuts in husk be de-husked as soon as possible?

options.text: Because the husk is worth more than the nut
So the shed can close early
Because dry husks are heavier
Because nuts in wet husk heat up and go mouldy

To trace the batch back to where it came from
To count the workers
To choose which bins to clean
